entities.name: Inca Empire
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Inca Empire's incorporation of the Bolivian altiplano (high plateau) around Lake Titicaca — the sacred heartland of Andean civilization and birthplace of Inca creation mythology — represents the empire's most spiritually significant territorial acquisition. Lake Titicaca (at 3,812 meters, the world's highest navigable lake) was where, according to Inca cosmology, the sun god Inti created the first Inca rulers Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo. The Tiwanaku civilization (300 BCE – 1000 CE), which preceded the Incas in the altiplano, bequeathed architectural techniques including the massive stone platform of Puma Punku that Inca engineers adapted.

The Bolivian altiplano's Aymara kingdoms (Lupaca, Colla, Charca) were conquered by Pachacuti and Topa Inca (1430s-1470s), incorporated as the Collasuyu quarter of the empire (the largest of the four Tawantinsuyu quarters by area). The altiplano's extreme altitude (Lake Titicaca basin at 3,800 meters) challenged Inca administrative systems but provided silver mines (Potosí and Porco) that funded the empire's military campaigns.

Potosí, discovered in 1545 by Spanish colonizers, produced 60% of the world's silver output between 1545-1800 — 45,000 tons — funding the Spanish Empire, triggering European inflation (the Price Revolution), and enabling global trade. The silver from the Bolivian altiplano financed the Spanish Armada, the Dutch East India Company's operations, and Chinese trade. Potosí's population reached 160,000 by 1650 — larger than London — making it the highest city and the first global commodity production center.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Inca Empire's Bolivian altiplano — through Potosí's 45,000 tons of silver production — financed the Spanish Empire, triggered the European Price Revolution, and created the first global commodity chain, making the Bolivian altiplano the site where the Inca Empire's legacy most permanently changed the world economy.
